details:
Lunar Mission Browser

Lunar Mission Browser is an interactive lunar mission-planning platform designed to help explore and evaluate potential landing locations, particularly around the lunar south pole. It brings lunar terrain visualization, celestial geometry, solar illumination, and Earth visibility into one unified interface.

Users can select candidate landing sites such as Shackleton Rim, Leibnitz Plateau, and Malapert Massif, choose an observation date and UTC time, and explore the Sun and Earth geometry relative to the selected location. The platform uses NASA NAIF SPICE resources for celestial calculations and provides terrain visualization and mission information through an interactive 3D interface.

The project aims to make complex lunar mission data easier to explore and understand. By bringing multiple environmental factors together, it can support preliminary landing-site assessment, educational exploration, and a better understanding of the challenges involved in planning future lunar missions.

Our technology stack includes React, Vite, and Three.js for the frontend; Python and FastAPI for the backend; and SpiceyPy, NumPy, Rasterio, and PyProj for scientific computing and geospatial processing. NASA NAIF SPICE kernels provide resources for celestial calculations, while the application supports lunar terrain data integration. The current demonstration terrain includes synthetic elevation data, which is clearly distinguished from real NASA LOLA data.

The creative aspect of the project is its integration of several mission-planning factors into a single interactive environment. Instead of examining terrain, sunlight, and Earth visibility separately, users can explore how these factors relate to a selected landing site and observation time.

During development, we considered scientific accuracy, coordinate reference frames, terrain coverage, data availability, usability, and the limitations of available datasets. We also designed the application to distinguish real scientific data from synthetic or unavailable information rather than presenting approximations as validated measurements.

Our intended impact is to make lunar mission-planning concepts more accessible and provide an extensible platform for exploring candidate landing locations and environmental conditions relevant to future lunar exploration.
